There’s a story about test screenings for a Mission Impossible movie. People kept complaining that the end went on too long. Kind of LOTR style in that you think it’s done but it’s not. It was the most consistent criticism of the film. So Cruise told them to put a single score over all the scenes. New test audiences suddenly loved the ending. 

That’s Nolan’s big trick. He uses extended montage-like sequences where he crosscuts between 2-5 things happening and adds a single score over it all. It makes it feel like there’s a lot happening and it’s all very important. It lends the films an (arguably unearned) energy that makes them feel much more meaningful and powerful than they usually are. 

It’s very fascinating to me. Especially with how many people say Interstellar is as good or better than 2001: a Space Odyssey. 2001 is so far beyond Interstellar. But Interstellar has the pacing trick that elevates what is very pedestrian filmmaking.

Downey’s character is Lewis Strauss.  Strauss was head of the AEC and was instrumental in denying Oppenheimer his security clearance.  

That’s in the movie and should be.  But the movie also tacks on about 45 minutes to show the Congressional hearing at which—well after the key events in the movie—Strauss was denied confirmation as Secretary of Commerce during the Eisenhower administration.  That’s a side note at best but most of the movie’s final act is about that hearing.  A needless segment.  Could have been cut in its entirety.  (Yes Downey does a great job with the role but the segment just doesn’t belong in the film.)

I certainly have criticisms of the film, but wow not these.

The bureau scenes are lower stakes. However they are set in a parallel structure to complement the themes and narratives in the other sections. Who safeguards the future of the nation? How do we decode the inscrutable thought process and tribal ethics of scientists? Because though their methods not often understood by the public or policymakers, the results certainly are. What does a country that is built out of self-interest look like (Strauss), what does a country built out of myopia look like (Oppenheimer pre-bomb), what does a country built from stewardship and communication look like (Oppenheimer post-bomb)? Nolan has done parallel narratives with all high stakes before, and in my opinion they have sometimes muddied the third act with too much business (Inception). In fairness though, he has also done movies with decidedly less balanced stakes with also not great results (civilian boat section of Dunkirk). 

Pugh's character is a real person, first off, and her history with Oppenheimer contributed to his character assassination at the security hearing. But she also reinforces a recurring question of theoretical and practical ideology. Oppenheimer lives in the theoretical world for the first two thirds of the film, carried by a sense of wanting to change the world but not considering consequences and real world effects. Part of this ideology relates to his connection with Tatlock: both his theoretical understanding of her socialist politics, but also his theoretical understanding of their relationship in isolation and in stasis, undisturbed by any of his actions or behavior. It isn't until Tatlock's suicide that Oppenheimer first understands the outcome of his actions in practice. She is also a foil to his relationship with Kitty; his and Tatlock's relationship is built on secrecy and non-communication. His relationship with Kitty eventually is built on trust and communication. This also reverberates with Oppenheimer's relationship with his colleagues and with the American people: relationships that begin with secrecy and inarticulation, but grow into transparency and involvement.

The bomb testing is a non-event in some ways because the eventual conclusion of the film is that it is a non-event, imo. The creation and detonation of the bomb, which required all this time and energy to steward, ends up paling in comparison to its repeated casual abuse and misuse. Two bombs in Japan, Russian tests in the Pacific, proliferation, and the development of an A-bomb. It turns out that as much energy and will goes into the creation of something, there's actually far more energy and thought and care that needs to be put in protecting its relationship with the world and the world's relationship to it in the fallout. Theoretical scientists like Oppenheimer and Edward Teller see a practical application of their work in the Trinity Test, but it's almost a light show for them. Unlike their more worldly peers, they do not see real practical effects, secondary effects, chain reactions, until it is too late.

I think wanting the bomb detonation to be a bigger, centerpiece event with a 35 second long explosion is a reasonable expectation for an audience to have, it was certainly my expectation. But having that would point to a movie with entirely different aims and idea as well. I suppose it sounds like that was the movie you'd have preferred watching, but this wasn't that movie and I think it sells it short a bit to judge it based on that movie's criteria.

**Oppenheimer** is by no reasonable standard a 'stinky pile of absolute dogshit'.

It is an intelligent, beautifully shot and tightly edited, biopic with some fine performances.  The Academy of Motion Picture Arts & Sciences does indeed award Oscars to biopics with predictable regularity - Mr. Attenborough's **Gandhi** (UK/1982) won eight Oscars.  That was a fine film that I have never met anyone who sat through it once say they were eager to view for a second time.  I suspect that Mr. Nolan's film will suffer a similar fate.

In general I agree with your criticisms and share your puzzlement concerning some of the historical events that Mr. Nolan devoted screen time to feature.  At best I'd go for 8/10.

I did watch the whole thing, and the technical aspects of the film were pretty good (cinematography, sound, editing), but afterward I couldn’t believe how much that movie made me disengage from what could have been a much better movie. All the stunt casting was distracting (is that Roderick from Diary of a Wimpy Kid) and was constantly pulling me out of the movie. Matt Damon’s character is portrayed as a buffoon instead of letting us recognize the evil inherent in that position, Jean Tatlock reduced to her sexuality, the lack of passion shown by Oppenheimer while simultaneously trying to tell us how passionate he is about everything, and trivializing how the government and industry worked to discredit socialists while embedding former nazis into our highest institutions post WWII. Nolan touches on a lot of ideas and leans into none of them, leaving me feeling meh about a lot of things that are crucial to the formation of our current world order. The more time that passes, the more I dislike this movie. I learned more about the mindsets of people during WWII from The Zone of Interest than from Oppenheimer’s mass scale tepid reflections. Severely overrated.

Reading what you wrote in the initial post, and that you responded two minutes after I commented, kinda makes me think that's not the case. You can certainly argue that there's too much in the movie to enjoy as a viewer, but the body of the post talks about not knowing why elements, including whole sections, were in the movie, and wanting more of the pyrotechnics.

Case in point - I read the biography before I saw the film. I was aware Pugh's character was a real person. And it covered a real aspect of Oppenheimer's life.

Nolan should have picked fewer aspects of the life and covered them more quickly and with more punch. Instead of making a sprawling snore fest.

I'm generally on board with the Nolan-bashing but I actually really enjoyed Oppenheimer and felt like it was a return to form after his most Nolany film, Tenet. Nolan's borderline-Randian focus on solitary heroes is usually a liability but Oppenheimer is one of only a handful of real, historical human beings who are maybe a good fit for that kind of treatment. He's a blue-blooded intellectual (clearly Nolan's favorite kind of person) who was actually brilliant in a technical sense and helmed a dangerous and secretive project of world-historical significance.

It actually works, as long as you're persuaded that the first nuclear bomb really meant a sea change for humankind and presented mind-boggling new ethical and technical problems (which I am, and OP probably isn't). It's a better use of the Nolan treatment than, I dunno, a guy who fights crime in a bat suit.

The problem, for me at least, was that I came away feeling that this very long film didn't tell me much that I didn't know about Mr. Oppenheimer when I first sat down - think of how different it was to watch **Lawrence of Arabia** for the first time (I left the theatre convinced that I knew that famous loon as well as I knew my oldest friend).
